CASE REPORTS / CASE SERIES
Postoperative hypotonia in a patient with stiff person syndrome:
a case report and literature review
Hypotonie postope´ratoire chez une patiente atteinte du «
syndrome de la personne raide » : pre ´sentation de cas et revue de
la litte´rature
Noha Elsherbini, DCS . Antonio Weingartshofer, MD . Steven B. Backman, MDCM, PhD, FRCPC
Received: 22 February 2022 / Revised: 2 May 2022 / Accepted: 4 May 2022 / Published online: 19 August 2022
/C211Canadian Anesthesiologists’ Society 2022
Abstract
Purpose Stiff person syndrome (SPS), an autoimmune
disease that manifests with episodic muscle rigidity and
spasms, has anesthetic considerations because
postoperative hypotonia may occur. This hypotonia has
been linked to muscle relaxants and volatile anesthetics
and may persist in spite of neostigmine administration and
train-of-four (TOF) monitoring suggesting full reversal.
We present a patient with SPS who experienced hypotonia
following total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA), which was
promptly reversed with sugammadex. These observations
are considered in light of the relevant medical literature.
Clinical features A 46-yr-old female patient with SPS
underwent breast lumpectomy and sentinel node biopsy.
Anesthesia consisted of TIVA (propofol/remifentanil) with
adjunctive administration of rocuronium 20 mg to obtain
adequate intubating conditions. Despite return of the TOF
ratio to 100% within 30 min, hypotonia was clinically
evident at conclusion of surgery two hours later.
Sugammadex 250 mg reversed residual muscle relaxation
permitting uneventful extubation. A literature review
identiﬁed six instances of postoperative hypotonia (TIVA,
n = 3; volatile anesthetics, n = 3) in spite of neostigmine
administration (n = 2) and TOF monitoring suggesting full
reversal (n = 4).
Conclusions Patients with SPS may show hypotonia
regardless of general anesthetic technique (TIVA vs
inhalational anesthesia), which can persist despite
recovery of the TOF ratio and may be more effectively
reversed by a chelating agent than with an
anticholinesterase. If general anesthesia is required, we
suggest a cautious approach to administering muscle
relaxants including using the smallest dose necessary,
considering the importance of clinical assessment of
muscle strength recovery in addition to TOF monitoring,
and discussing postoperative ventilation risk with the
patient prior to surgery.

stiff person syndrome
Stiff person syndrome (SPS), ﬁrst described in 1956, is a
rare progressive autoimmune disease with a prevalence of
approximately 1/1,000,000. It is characterized by
involuntary, sudden-onset, muscle rigidity, and spasm
that may be precipitated by various triggers such as
touch, noxious stimuli, or emotional stress. Stiff person
syndrome is thought to be mediated by antibodies to
glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) isoenzyme 65, which is
involved in the production of gamma-aminobutyric acid
(GABA), with subsequent reduction in central GABAergic
transmission. As GABA is a major inhibitory
neurotransmitter, it is postulated that this reduction
results in excessive neuronal activity including an
augmented motor neuron drive manifesting as muscle
spasm and rigidity.
1,2
A few case reports have described the anesthetic care
provided to patients with SPS. Unpredictably, some
patients may experience postoperative hypotonia of
variable severity and duration (Table 1).3–7 While muscle
weakness is a known consequence of muscle relaxants, the
consensus is that a propofol-based anesthetic (i.e., total
intravenous anesthesia [TIVA]) vs inhalational anesthesia
is a better choice for general anesthesia maintenance
because volatile anesthetics may contribute to the
postoperative hypotonia.
8–10
We report postoperative hypotonia in a patient with SPS
following surgery under general anesthesia (TIVA) and
compare our observations with those of case studies
identiﬁed in a literature review.
Case report
Informed consent was obtained from the patient to publish
this report. A 46-yr-old female (165 cm, 70 kg) with SPS
was scheduled for a lumpectomy and sentinel lymph node
biopsy following diagnosis of breast (left) cancer. Six years

prior to surgery she was diagnosed with SPS that
manifested as muscle spasms and episodes of rigidity
provoked by anxiety or by certain activities such as
stretching. Investigation for SPS conﬁrmed elevated GAD
antibodies in her cerebrospinal ﬂuid (anti-GAD antibodies
[ 100), and at the time of surgery her medical treatment
included oral diazepam 5 mg and azathioprine 50 mg twice
daily. Baclofen was discontinued by her neurologist two
years prior to surgery, and she had received monthly iv
immunoglobulin therapy for 1.5 years (last treatment ﬁve
years prior to surgery). Her last SPS exacerbation, one year
prior to surgery, was thought to be triggered by work-
related anxiety. Concomitant medical conditions included
type I diabetes (blood glucose well-controlled; no
symptoms of peripheral neuropathy in upper or lower
extremities), generalized anxiety disorder and
gastroesophageal reﬂux. Non SPS-related medications
included insulin and pantoprazole. She was a non-smoker
and had no cardiovascular or respiratory comorbidities. She
had no prior surgical history. One month prior to surgery, a
neurologic exam (requested by the surgeon for baseline
functional assessment) identiﬁed only mild limitations of
neck movement and shoulder abduction.
The patient was interviewed in the preoperative clinic
three days before surgery (S. B. B). On physical exam, the
airway was reassuring (normal range of motion of head,
neck, and jaw; normal thyromental distance; full set of
teeth; Mallampati 2) and laboratory ﬁndings (complete
blood count, blood chemistry, coagulation proﬁle) as well
as an electrocardiogram (EKG) were within normal
parameters. The patient was well informed about
anesthesia-related SPS concerns including the risk of
postoperative hypotonia following general anesthesia.

The option of a strictly regional/local anesthesia technique
was not discussed as experience with this approach (for
combined breast surgery and axillary lymph node
dissection) is lacking at our hospital.
Following insertion of an 18G catheter into a right
upper-extremity vein (left arm draped for surgery),
standard monitors were applied (3-lead EKG, noninvasive
blood pressure cuff [lower limb so as to not interfere with
intravenous infusions], pulse oximeter, Bispectral Index
TM
(BISTM; Covidien/Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN, USA)
monitor electrodes, and train-of-four (TOF) monitor
(Philips [Amsterdam, the Netherlands] 865383 IntelliVue
Neuromuscular Transmission module accelerometer
afﬁxed to thumb; ulnar nerve stimulation, no thumb pre-
load). Premedication consisted of midazolam 2.0 mg
(anxiolytic) and glycopyrrolate 0.3 mg (antisialagogue)
while the patient was preoxygenated with 100% oxygen via
a snug-ﬁtting face mask. Loss of consciousness was
achieved with propofol 200 mg, lidocaine 80 mg,
sufentanil 15 lg, and remifentanil 100 lg; this was
followed by dexamethasone 8 mg for postoperative
nausea and vomiting (PONV) prophylaxis and
clindamycin 600 mg. Although bag-and-mask ventilation
was performed without difﬁculty, insertion of the
laryngoscope blade into the oropharynx required
facilitation with 20 mg rocuronium; TOF calibration was
done just prior to rocuronium administration.
Subsequently, oral intubation was easily achieved (grade
2 Cormack–Lehane view, #7.0 endotracheal tube). General
anesthesia was maintained by continuous infusion of
propofol (100–200 lg/C1kg

(0.1 lg/C1kg-1/C1min-1, titrated to maintain systemic arterial
pressure within 20% of baseline. No additional muscle
relaxant was administered to help ensure that nerves could
be identiﬁed during axillary lymph node dissection by
electrocautery-elicited muscle contraction. Normothermia
was maintained with a lower-body forced-air warming
blanket.
Maintenance of an appropriate depth of anesthesia and
stability of cardiovascular parameters during surgery were
achieved without incident. Train-of-four returned to 4/4
(100%) within 30 min of rocuronium administration. The
surgery was uneventful and lasted one hour and 45 min, at
which time the infusions were discontinued. Ondansetron
4 mg was administered for further PONV prophylaxis.
Upon emergence, the patient followed commands but had a
weak hand grip, was unable to lift her head or extremities,
and spontaneous ventilation consisted of shallow tidal
volumes (50–150 ml). Sugammadex 250 mg was then
administered and reversal of muscle weakness was
observed within about two minutes. The patient was
subsequently extubated in the operating room and
transferred to the postanesthesia care unit without
incident. The patient was discharged home a few hours
afterwards. Follow-up four days later revealed a smooth
postoperative course at home without exacerbation of SPS
symptoms or any sign of muscle weakness.
Literature review
We identiﬁed sixteen reports concerned with the use of
muscle relaxants in patients with SPS (Table 1).
Postoperative hypotonia was described in ﬁve patients
(two events in one patient on different occasions), which
was associated with administration of muscle relaxants
including succinylcholine,
3 vecuronium,3,5 atracurium,4
pancuronium,7 and rocuronium. 6 Volatile anesthetics,
used on three occasions (twice in the same patient 3,4),
were hypothesized to contribute to the hypotonia.
Nevertheless, hypotonia was also observed in three cases
where TIVA was used.
5–7 The hypotonia persisted in spite
of reversal with neostigmine 3,4 and TOF monitoring
suggesting adequate reversal. 3–6 The hypotonia can be of
sufﬁcient magnitude to require prolonged respiratory
support (i.e., intubation and mechanical ventilation). 3–7
Discussion
We present a patient with SPS who underwent surgery
under TIVA. Despite return of the TOF ratio to 100%
within 30 min after a small dose of rocuronium, hypotonia
was clinically evident after conclusion of surgery two
hours later. Following reversal of muscle relaxation
(sugammadex), the patient was easily extubated. This
report highlights that patients with SPS anesthetized with a
TIVA technique can be sensitive to muscle relaxants and,
despite full recovery of the TOF ratio, may still require
muscle relaxant reversal.
Stiff person syndrome is a rare, progressive,
autoimmune disorder of the central nervous system more
commonly observed in females than males (approximately
2:1). The spasmodic muscle contractions are often painful
and may eventually progress to loss of mobility. Muscle
spasms can be evoked by ordinary sensory stimuli or
emotional stress, and patients may show debilitating
anticipatory anxiety and task-speciﬁc phobias.
Simultaneous contraction of agonist and antagonist
muscle groups and continuous involuntary ﬁring of motor
units at rest are hallmarks of this disease. Stiff person
syndrome can be associated with other autoimmune
conditions such as type 1 diabetes, and several variations

have been described (e.g., stiff limb syndrome, jerking man
syndrome, and paraneoplastic and cerebellar variants).
1,2
While impaired central GABAergic transmission,
secondary to GAD antibodies, is thought to account for
the muscle spasm, not all SPS patients show elevated
antibodies to GAD, and most individuals with elevated
GAD antibodies do not show SPS symptoms. Thus,
elevated GAD antibodies are neither necessary nor
sufﬁcient to account for SPS symptoms. Moreover,
patients with SPS may also show high titers of antibodies
against other central nervous system proteins implicated in
neural transmission, including GABA-receptor-associated
protein, ampiphysin, and gephyrin.
1,2
While there is no cure for SPS, muscle spasms may be
reduced by boosting central GABAergic transmission with
oral administration of baclofen, a GABAB receptor agonist,
and diazepam, a GABA A receptor agonist. In cases of
severe disease, intrathecal injection of baclofen can be
considered. As with other autoimmune disorders, treatment
with intravenous immunoglobulin, corticosteroids,
plasmapheresis, and immunosuppressive agents has been
described.
2
The hypotonia we observed with only 20 mg
rocuronium (approx. 0.3 mg /C1kg-1) at two hours is
noteworthy, considering that even with more than twice
this dose full spontaneous recovery should be apparent by
100 min.
11 The brisk recovery of muscle strength following
sugammadex administration directly links the weakness to
a lingering muscle relaxant effect. This is consistent with
previous reports suggesting a heightened sensitivity to
various nondepolarizing muscle relaxants in some patients
(Table 1);
3–7 there is less (and also conﬂicting) experience
with succinylcholine (Table 1).3,12 The
mechanism(s) mediating sensitivity to muscle relaxants is
123
Anesthesia and stiff person syndrome 1423

unknown. Possibly, it may involve downregulation of
nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction
secondary to an autoimmune response reminiscent of
myasthenia gravis 13 or to prolonged, excessive release of
acetylcholine from motor neuron terminals 14 mediating the
muscle spasms. We emphasize that caution is exercised
when administering muscle relaxants to patients with SPS
including using the smallest dose necessary and that the
risk of postoperative ventilation must be discussed with the
patient prior to surgery.
Regarding a possible inﬂuence of anesthetic drugs, early
reports speculated that volatiles may contribute to
postoperative muscle weakness in patients with SPS by
enhancing central GABAergic transmission, and that this
effect may be exaggerated in patients treated with
baclofen.
3,4 Recommendations have been made to reduce
or avoid volatile drug administration in patients with
SPS8–10 even though hypotonia has also been reported
following TIVA.5–7 Our case provides further evidence that
hypotonia may occur in patients with SPS following
TIVA—even when baclofen is not a confounding
medication.
Another unusual feature we observed was the failure of
TOF monitoring to predict recovery: the TOF ratio was
100% even though the patient was clinically too weak for
extubation. Previous reports also indicate unreliability of
TOF monitoring in patients with SPS,
3–6 although
quantitative data are only reported in one case. 6 With our
case, neuromuscular monitoring was via accelerometry,
which can exaggerate the TOF ratio compared with
electromyography.
15 Moreover, even in normal patients,
TOF monitoring (of any type) may overestimate the return
of full muscle strength and when neuromuscular
monitoring indicates recovery, muscle relaxants may still
occupy as many as 75% of acetylcholine receptors.
16
Corresponding information concerned with the safety
factor of neuromuscular transmission and the relationship
of the TOF response to muscle strength in patients with
SPS is unknown. We emphasize the importance of clinical
assessment of muscle strength, in addition to TOF
monitoring, prior to extubation in this unique patient
population.
This is the second report where sugammadex
successfully reversed muscle paralysis
17 while other cases
describe persistent hypotonia in spite of reversal attempts
with neostigmine.
3,4 Prudence is required when trying to
interpret these observations in such a small number of
patients. Nevertheless, this may indicate that reversal of
muscle paralytics via cholinesterase inhibitors is not as
reliable as that achieved with irreversible chelating agents
in patients with SPS.
Anesthetic management in our case consisted of TIVA,
endotracheal intubation facilitated by a muscle relaxant and
mechanical ventilation. Other strategies may be
considered. For example, airway management could have
been achieved with a supraglottic airway device.
Advantages include the possible avoidance of muscle
relaxant and decreased dose of induction drugs.
Disadvantages include less deﬁnitive airway control if
postoperative ventilation is required, and the risk of
aspiration secondary to the patient’s gastroesophageal
reﬂux comorbidity. Another possible strategy could have
been regional anesthesia. Advantages include avoidance of
general anesthesia and muscle relaxants, assuming
adequate intraoperative analgesia. Disadvantages include
heavy sedation, which may be required to blunt anxiety

that can trigger SPS-related muscle spasms. In addition,
this strategy requires specialized experience (anesthesia
and surgical) that may not be available. For patients with
SPS, notwithstanding the relative scarcity of cases, there
are no known contraindications to anesthetic drugs with the
caveat of a cautious approach to using muscle relaxants
(above). Various case reports describing the successful use
of iv sedation and/or peripheral blocks have been
published, with emphasis on alleviating anxiety that may
trigger muscle spasms.
9,10 Neuraxial anesthesia (spinal
and/or epidural) has also been described, although spine
deformity and muscle spasms may pose technical
challenges.
9,10 As with any patient, the anesthesia
strategy must take into account the patient’s underlying
condition(s) and medications, surgical procedure, available
resources and expertise, and, of course, the patient’s
wishes.
Our case report adds to the SPS literature showing that
hypotonia may be observed in patients who receive TIVA,
can persist despite full recovery of the TOF ratio, and may
be more effectively reversed by a chelating agent than with
an anticholinesterase. We emphasize that caution is
exercised when administering muscle relaxants to patients
with SPS, including using the smallest dose necessary,
considering the importance of clinical assessment of
muscle strength recovery in addition to TOF monitoring,
and discussing the risk of postoperative ventilation with the
patient prior to surgery.

Anesthesia and stiff person syndrome 1425

segments.text:
A 46-yr-old female (165 cm, 70 kg) with SPS
was scheduled for a lumpectomy and sentinel lymph node
biopsy following diagnosis of breast (left) cancer. Six years
segments.evidence: Deterministic clinical-window selection for Stage 07 single-case v1.

segments.text:
prior to surgery she was diagnosed with SPS that
manifested as muscle spasms and episodes of rigidity
provoked by anxiety or by certain activities such as
stretching. Investigation for SPS conﬁrmed elevated GAD
antibodies in her cerebrospinal ﬂuid (anti-GAD antibodies
[ 100), and at the time of surgery her medical treatment
included oral diazepam 5 mg and azathioprine 50 mg twice
daily. Baclofen was discontinued by her neurologist two
years prior to surgery, and she had received monthly iv
immunoglobulin therapy for 1.5 years (last treatment ﬁve
years prior to surgery). Her last SPS exacerbation, one year
prior to surgery, was thought to be triggered by work-
related anxiety. Concomitant medical conditions included
type I diabetes (blood glucose well-controlled; no
symptoms of peripheral neuropathy in upper or lower
extremities), generalized anxiety disorder and
gastroesophageal reﬂux. Non SPS-related medications
included insulin and pantoprazole. She was a non-smoker
and had no cardiovascular or respiratory comorbidities. She
had no prior surgical history. One month prior to surgery, a
neurologic exam (requested by the surgeon for baseline
functional assessment) identiﬁed only mild limitations of
neck movement and shoulder abduction.
The patient was interviewed in the preoperative clinic
three days before surgery (S. B. B). On physical exam, the
airway was reassuring (normal range of motion of head,
neck, and jaw; normal thyromental distance; full set of
teeth; Mallampati 2) and laboratory ﬁndings (complete
blood count, blood chemistry, coagulation proﬁle) as well
as an electrocardiogram (EKG) were within normal
parameters. The patient was well informed about
anesthesia-related SPS concerns including the risk of
postoperative hypotonia following general anesthesia.
segments.evidence: Deterministic clinical-window selection for Stage 07 single-case v1.

segments.text:
The option of a strictly regional/local anesthesia technique
was not discussed as experience with this approach (for
combined breast surgery and axillary lymph node
dissection) is lacking at our hospital.
Following insertion of an 18G catheter into a right
upper-extremity vein (left arm draped for surgery),
standard monitors were applied (3-lead EKG, noninvasive
blood pressure cuff [lower limb so as to not interfere with
intravenous infusions], pulse oximeter, Bispectral Index
TM
(BISTM; Covidien/Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN, USA)
monitor electrodes, and train-of-four (TOF) monitor
(Philips [Amsterdam, the Netherlands] 865383 IntelliVue
Neuromuscular Transmission module accelerometer
afﬁxed to thumb; ulnar nerve stimulation, no thumb pre-
load). Premedication consisted of midazolam 2.0 mg
(anxiolytic) and glycopyrrolate 0.3 mg (antisialagogue)
while the patient was preoxygenated with 100% oxygen via
a snug-ﬁtting face mask. Loss of consciousness was
achieved with propofol 200 mg, lidocaine 80 mg,
sufentanil 15 lg, and remifentanil 100 lg; this was
followed by dexamethasone 8 mg for postoperative
nausea and vomiting (PONV) prophylaxis and
clindamycin 600 mg. Although bag-and-mask ventilation
was performed without difﬁculty, insertion of the
laryngoscope blade into the oropharynx required
facilitation with 20 mg rocuronium; TOF calibration was
done just prior to rocuronium administration.
Subsequently, oral intubation was easily achieved (grade
2 Cormack–Lehane view, #7.0 endotracheal tube). General
anesthesia was maintained by continuous infusion of
propofol (100–200 lg/C1kg
-1/C1min-1, titrated to BIS values
between 40 and 60) and remifentanil infusion
segments.evidence: Deterministic clinical-window selection for Stage 07 single-case v1.

segments.text:
(0.1 lg/C1kg-1/C1min-1, titrated to maintain systemic arterial
pressure within 20% of baseline. No additional muscle
relaxant was administered to help ensure that nerves could
be identiﬁed during axillary lymph node dissection by
electrocautery-elicited muscle contraction. Normothermia
was maintained with a lower-body forced-air warming
blanket.
Maintenance of an appropriate depth of anesthesia and
stability of cardiovascular parameters during surgery were
achieved without incident. Train-of-four returned to 4/4
(100%) within 30 min of rocuronium administration. The
surgery was uneventful and lasted one hour and 45 min, at
which time the infusions were discontinued. Ondansetron
4 mg was administered for further PONV prophylaxis.
Upon emergence, the patient followed commands but had a
weak hand grip, was unable to lift her head or extremities,
and spontaneous ventilation consisted of shallow tidal
volumes (50–150 ml). Sugammadex 250 mg was then
administered and reversal of muscle weakness was
observed within about two minutes. The patient was
subsequently extubated in the operating room and
transferred to the postanesthesia care unit without
incident. The patient was discharged home a few hours
afterwards. Follow-up four days later revealed a smooth
postoperative course at home without exacerbation of SPS
symptoms or any sign of muscle weakness.
